Author: tholin
Content: Even if you got those high speed interfaces on a gf180 chip, there is nothing you can put on that chip to generate or process data at those speeds.

Author: tholin
Content: WCH makes a chip that is a PCIe to RS232 adapter (just a PCIe version of their popular USBTTL chips). If you put that on a board with a gf180mcu SoC and set it to one of the higher supported UART rates, i.e. 500000bps, you’d have all the throughput you need.

Author: tholin
Content: To share my personal experience: I taped out a RISC-V core on GFMPW-1, about as performant as a non-pipelined core could get, and wired it up to a SPI <-> 10/100mbps ethernet bridge (enc28j60) and the system kept dropping packets because the RISC-V CPU struggled to process them faster than they were coming in.

Author: tholin
Content: Like, it’d frequently die during IPv6 SLAAC or IPv4 DHCP because the broadcast responses combined with background broadcast traffic on my home network overflowed the buffer.

Author: tholin
Content: So, 10/100mbps ethernet on gf180mcu would make sense, but then you’re hitting data processing speed limits anyways.

Author: rebelmike
Content:
I don’t think I’ve even pushed the repo to GitHub yet. But the main things I’ve done:
Use FemtoRV as the core.
2 clocks per instruction for all instructions except memory access and branches. Predictable performance in general to allow cycle counting. No C extension.
Add some B extension instructions. In particular I found rotates being missing a problem when writing for BIO as it meant you couldn’t easily shift bits out to an arbitrary pin. Bit and byte reverse. And the logical ops with one inverted operand.

Author: rebelmike
Content: One note, so far this is a rewrite. I haven’t been referencing the original BIO implementation, just the spec. So possibly this would be a good point to try and transplant what I have into the original BIO implementation, especially if this project might be gaining a deadline.

Author: namibj
Content:
the base "muxed e-test" is just an analog switch matrix on the same die as a bunch of DUTs; a simple digital decoder selects one DUT, activates those switches and deactivates the others; there's two wires to each DUT "LEF pin"; off-chip multimeters are then scripted/remote-controlled to sample a few hundred/thousand "interesting" bias conditions of the DUT; then the mux is changed to select the next DUT; then this repeats; after a few minutes the setup rings a bell/buzzer/status-light and a nearby human swaps in the next COB at convenience; this allows measuring hundreds of dies under DC operating point conditions without very expensive raw wafer probe stations.

_Might_ repeat it afterwards with the test chip and it's socket-board in a freezer and/or oven or if thermal mass works out small enough a 2/3 stage peltier chamber might even give the essentially-full specification range of die temperatures without being a genuinely expensive chamber and without the human having to touch each chip once for each temperature.

The big things are just that thin oxide nvt NMOS have zero SPICE and zero e-test data (at least NDA-free), a bunch of stuff has zero local mismatch statistical models, that latter includes (notably!) plain vias which promise a factor of over 3 from typ to max and no min (breaks predictable matching of differential pair resistor divider kind-of structures, without spending a bunch of space and parasticic capacitance on spamming vias in hopes of the unspecified statistics being the type that's persuaded by such tricks).
